The call was made at the 2026 Africa Leadership and Impact Summit, themed “Breaking Barriers: From Vision to Execution,” and tagged Beyond 2.0, Abuja today.
Speaking at the summit, the Convener, A.S. Yunusa, said the gathering was designed to connect minds, exchange ideas and inspire participants to move beyond discussions to meaningful action.
He said although many people had ideas about building businesses, leading organisations and transforming communities, having a vision was only the beginning, stressing the need to translate such ambitions into measurable results.
“The real challenge is moving from what we imagine to what we actually accomplish. That is exactly what brought us here today. We want to go beyond talking about possibilities. We want to discover how to turn ideas into action,” he said.
Yunusa added that leadership went beyond having a vision and executing plans, describing it as the ability to provide direction to people and effectively manage available resources.
According to him, the ability to convert acquired knowledge into productivity remains one of the most important skills required to achieve meaningful progress.
“Knowledge must be translated into better decisions, productivity and problem-solving. When you are able to convert what you have acquired into productivity, you will see the difference,” he said.
Yunusa identified the knowledge-action gap as one of the major obstacles preventing many Africans from turning their ambitions into tangible achievements.
Other challenges, he said, included fear of failure, resistance to change, lack of structure and accountability, as well as limited mentorship and exposure.
He observed that many people could articulate problems effectively but struggled to deliver results because they lacked the practical skills required to execute tasks.
The convener also identified excessive dependence on digital screens and the pressure of information abundance as challenges confronting young people.
He said although technology had made information readily accessible, many young people were increasingly comparing their lives with lifestyles displayed on social media rather than concentrating on building their own capacities.
“Information is abundant. It is giving you pressure. That pressure is what you think is a mental health problem, because you are comparing yourself with what others are doing,” he said.
Citing statistics, Yunusa said between 80 and 90 per cent of New Year resolutions were never achieved, while only 19.7 per cent were sustained until the end of the year.
He added that between 70 and 80 per cent of organisational strategies also failed, largely because of poor implementation and inadequate accountability.
He stressed that effective execution required templates, documentation, systems and structures that would ensure continuity even in the absence of organisational leaders.
Yunusa urged participants to concentrate on issues within their control and influence rather than expend energy on circumstances they could not change.
He said individuals and organisations must develop practical strategies to manage external challenges while remaining focused on achieving their objectives.
Also speaking, a guest speaker, Osilama E. Osilama, said progress required courage, innovation and calculated risks, noting that individuals must be willing to step outside their comfort zones to achieve meaningful success.
“Your richness in life is proportional to the amount of risk you are ready to take. If you are not ready to take risk, life cannot help you. You must be a risk-taker, but a calculated risk-taker. Make sure the risk is worth taking,” he said.
He urged participants to embrace disruption and innovation, warning that familiar practices could become obstacles when they no longer produced the desired results.
Osilama said successful execution required clearly defined objectives, timelines, resources, responsibilities and performance measures.
He added that accountability, both to oneself and others, was essential for achieving sustainable results, regardless of an individual’s competence.
He challenged participants to move from spectatorship to productivity through five fundamental shifts: from consumer to creator; inspiration to implementation; ambition to execution; individual success to institutional impact; and visibility to value creation.
He cautioned young people against confusing social media popularity with genuine influence, saying competence, problem-solving and meaningful contributions were the true measures of leadership.
Osilama advised young people to be deliberate in choosing mentors, warning that associating with individuals whose character was questionable could negatively influence their personal and professional development.
One of the parcipants Lucky Erherka, said the programme changed the mindset from planning to execution, adding that she would apply the lessons in her community to create impact.
He urged aspiring entrepreneurs to acquire the necessary knowledge and understand the principles guiding their chosen industries before venturing into business.
